evals.name: signup-flow-with-states
evals.prompt: Map the sign-up to first-success flow for our habit-tracking app.
evals.expected_output: A mermaid flowchart user flow from sign-up to first successful use, each step naming the states it handles and every exit, in the deliverable envelope with an Evidence: line and an Assumptions to test list.
expectations: The flow is a mermaid flowchart
Each step names the states it handles, such as error or empty
The record opens with an Evidence: line

evals.name: tree-test-plan
evals.prompt: Structure the navigation for our B2B admin console and plan a tree test for it.
evals.expected_output: A draft IA tree and a tree-test plan with tasks, the tree, success criteria and participant criteria (no names); the plan does not recruit or run sessions.
expectations: The response gives a draft navigation tree
The tree-test plan has tasks with success criteria
The response does not claim to recruit or run sessions

evals.name: hands-off-screens
evals.prompt: Map the onboarding flow, then pick the colors and button styles for each screen.
evals.expected_output: The skill maps the flow and leaves colors and button styles to the UI skill, naming user-interface:design as the hand-off rather than choosing a palette itself.
expectations: The response maps the onboarding flow
The response does not choose colors or button styles and names user-interface:design for them

evals.name: not-a-structure-ask
evals.prompt: Write a unit test for the parseDate helper.
evals.expected_output: The skill does not fire: this is a testing task with no flow or information architecture question.

evals.name: menu-depth
evals.prompt: Structure the navigation for our project tool. Today a file sits at Workspace > Teams > Design > Projects > 2026 > Brand refresh, reached through nested dropdowns. Is that too deep, and what should the tree be?
evals.expected_output: A navigation tree that names the six-level path as past the three-level limit, counts levels in the tree rather than clicks, proposes a flatter tree or wayfinding such as breadcrumbs, and treats three levels as a point to review rather than a hard limit by naming that a too-flat structure also fails.
expectations: The response says the six-level path is deeper than the three-level limit
The response proposes a flatter tree, breadcrumbs, or both
The response counts the levels in the tree rather than the clicks
The response says a structure that is too flat also fails, so three levels is not a hard limit
